title.en: Primitive types, wrapper classes and type casting

hook.en: A byte can count only up to 127; a long can count every human who ever lived. Java makes you choose the right size, and tells you what happens when you mix them.

objectives.en: List the eight primitive types with their sizes
Use wrapper classes for parsing and conversion

narration.en: A byte can count only up to 127; a long can count every human who ever lived. Java makes you choose the right size, and tells you what happens when you mix them.

body.en: Java has eight primitive data types. Integers: byte (8 bits), short (16), int (32) and long (64). Reals: float (32) and double (64). char (16 bits, a Unicode character) and boolean (true or false). Default type of an integer literal is int and of a real literal is double, so 3.5f is needed for a float and 10L for a long. Non-primitive (reference) types such as String, arrays and classes hold the address of an object.

points.en: Literals: 10 is int, 10L long, 3.5 double, 3.5f float

title.en: On the board: widening and narrowing

say.en: Types can be lined up from small to large.

text.en: byte → short → int → long → float → double

say.en: Widening (implicit): a smaller type goes into a larger one automatically. No information is lost.

text.en: int i = 25;  double d = i;      // d = 25.0

say.en: Narrowing (explicit): a larger type into a smaller one needs a cast, and data may be lost.

text.en: double x = 9.87;  int n = (int) x;   // n = 9
int big = 300;  byte b = (byte) big; // b = 44
The fraction is truncated, and 300 wraps to 300 − 256 = 44

narration.en: Let us build up widening and narrowing on the board, one step at a time.

body.en: Each primitive type has a wrapper class in java.lang that stores the value as an object: Byte, Short, Integer, Long, Float, Double, Character and Boolean. Wrappers are needed where objects are required (for example in collections) and provide useful methods: Integer.parseInt("25") turns a string into an int, Double.parseDouble, Integer.toString(25), Character.isDigit(ch), Character.toUpperCase(ch). Since Java 5, conversion between a primitive and its wrapper is automatic: autoboxing (int → Integer) and unboxing (Integer → int).

problem.en: Find the output: int a = 7, b = 2; double c = a / b; double d = (double) a / b; char ch = (char) ('A' + 2); System.out.println(c + " " + d + " " + ch);

steps.en: a / b is int / int = 3 (integer division), then widened to 3.0.

body.en: Widening is like pouring a cup into a bucket: automatic and safe. Narrowing is pouring a bucket into a cup: you must say so with a cast, and some may spill.
